title: Careful words (Avot 1:9)
hookLine: Simeon ben Shetach: question witnesses well, and guard your words so no one learns to lie
carry: a question can teach a lie
last: KINDNESS ISN'T THE SAME AS CLOSENESS.

lines: THE QUESTION HANDED HIM THE ANSWER.
cards: A kid is standing in the kitchen with crumbs on his shirt, and a parent asks, you didn't take the last cookie, did you? And the kid, who is not a fool, says no. The question handed him the answer.
It told him which story would get him out of trouble. Questions like that get asked at home, at work, in a group chat.
Long ago, a judge in Jerusalem noticed the same thing in a courtroom, where the stakes were a lot higher than a cookie.

teach.b: The judge is Simeon ben Shetach, who with his partner Judah ben Tabbai makes up one of the pairs of teachers in the chain of Pirkei Avot.
He led the court in a stormy time, and later tradition remembers him as fearless in front of kings. His saying, in chapter one, comes in two halves.
First: examine the witnesses thoroughly. The Torah says a matter is established by two or three witnesses, and Simeon wants them questioned hard, because a careless court convicts the innocent.

teach.h: YOUR QUESTION CAN TEACH THE LIE.
teach.b: Then the surprising half: and be careful with your words, so that they don't learn from them to lie. That half isn't aimed at the witnesses. It's aimed at the judge.
If the judge asks, was the knife in his right hand, the witness now knows the court is looking for a knife in a right hand. The question teaches the lie.
So the careful judge asks open questions, and lets the story come out on its own. The Talmud tells a story that shows how seriously Simeon took this.
He once saw a man chase another man into a ruin. He ran in after them and found one man dying and the other holding a bloody sword. And Simeon said, in effect: either you killed him, or I did.
But I can't convict you. The Torah needs two witnesses, and I only saw the sword, not the blow. Even when he was sure, he held himself to the court's rule.
Questions shape what people tell you, and what you say you saw becomes someone else's truth.

how: Jewish law built strict rules for testimony on this teaching: witnesses are questioned separately and closely, and Avot 1:9 is also read as a guide to honest speech well beyond the courtroom.

o: speaking politely so no one is ever offended
keeping every promise you make out loud
asking questions that don't hint at the answer

games.q: what's inside the saying — tap the pairs.
p: a judge who led the court

s: the second half of the saying is aimed at the witnesses
it's aimed at the judge: his own questions can teach a witness how to lie.
the Torah needs more than one witness to establish a matter
two or three witnesses, which is why Simeon couldn't convict the man with the sword.
Simeon convicted the man he found holding the sword
in the Talmud's story he said he could not, because he alone had seen, and not the blow.

games.q: you're Simeon ben Shetach. you find a dying man and another man holding a bloody sword. you're the only one who saw. what do you do?
o: convict him yourself. you know what happened.
say you can't convict him on one witness.
find someone to say they saw it too.
games.why: in the Talmud's story he says either you or I killed him, but the Torah needs two witnesses. he held his own words to the court's standard.

practice: Think of a conversation coming up where you want the truth, with a child, a coworker, a friend, and notice the question you'd normally ask, the one with the answer tucked inside it.
Now, slowly, turn it into an open one: not, you finished it, right? Just, how did it go? Say it silently a few times, until it feels natural.

wordCard.voice: Careful words. Simeon ben Shetach's warning to judges: the way you ask can teach someone how to lie.

orig.note: Mishnaic Hebrew: be careful with your words.
